prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Greece, Medea, Jesmyn

outputs.L1:
“In ancient Greece, for all her heroes, for Medea ... water meant death.”  
— Jesmyn Ward, *Salvage the Bones*

I poured a bowl of cereal and threw the empty box in the trash can. Granddaddy pulled the box from the trash, poured the crumbs into a bowl, then doused the sand in milk. He looked down at the bowl, murmuring about how he had survived the Depression. He told a story about asking for hot water at colored diners, how he would pour ketchup into cups to make soup. This was how I first learned I am wasteful.

•

I would stand in the bathroom with my mother. I would ask her why the water in the bowl was red. She would tell me she had eaten beets. I suppose I was too young to learn the truth: milkflowers spill petals red.

•

In my Catholic school of fish, we took a beautifully wrapped box and passed it around the class, unwrapping it piece by piece. Afterwards, it was cleverly explained that the box was a girl’s virginity, the gift we give our husbands. And who wants a toy that has already been opened? Half the joy is in untying the string. This is how I was taught that, at my very core, I am ungrateful.

•

I met someone recently, in an Irish bar, who told me it’s about knowing what I need. He said later, what you need is a wife.
outputs.L2:
“In old Greece, despite all its champions, for Medea ... water signified dying.” — Jesmyn Ward, *Salvage the Bones*

I fixed myself cereal, then dropped the emptied carton into the garbage. My grandfather reached into the can, took the box back out, shook the remaining dust and fragments into a dish, and soaked that sandy residue with milk. Staring into the bowl, he muttered about making it through the Depression. He told me how, in Black-only diners, he would request hot water and stir ketchup into cups of it, turning it into soup. That was my first lesson that I wasted things.  

•  

I used to stand beside my mother in the bathroom and ask why the water in the toilet had turned red. She would say she had been eating beets. I guess I was still too little to be told what was really happening: milkflowers shedding crimson petals.  

•  

At my Catholic school, in our school of fish, the class was handed a gorgeously wrapped present. We passed it from student to student, removing the wrapping layer by layer. Then the lesson was neatly revealed: the box stood for a girl’s virginity, the offering meant for her future husband. After all, who wants a plaything that has been opened already? Part of the delight is loosening the ribbon yourself. That was how I was instructed to believe that, in the deepest part of me, I lacked gratitude.  

•  

Not long ago, I met a man in an Irish pub who said the point was understanding what I needed. Later, he told me: what you need is a wife.
outputs.L3:
The speaker’s understanding of scarcity and wastefulness begins with her grandfather’s memories of surviving the Depression. Through his stories, she learns that nothing should be taken for granted and that waste is a serious moral failure. His experiences create a household atmosphere in which material things—food, money, clothing, and opportunities—must be carefully preserved. What may seem ordinary or abundant to a child is framed through the older generation’s memory of deprivation.

Alongside this lesson in scarcity, the speaker recalls her childhood confusion about menstruation. Rather than explaining the truth directly, her mother shields her from knowledge about her own body. This silence turns a natural process into something mysterious and possibly shameful. The speaker is not given the language or understanding she needs, and as a result, her developing sense of womanhood is shaped by secrecy and embarrassment.

Her Catholic schooling reinforces these feelings by teaching her that female virginity is a precious gift meant to be saved for a future husband. In this environment, a girl’s body is not presented as fully her own. Instead, it is treated as something that must be protected, preserved, and eventually given away within the boundaries of marriage. The emphasis on purity teaches the speaker that her value is tied to restraint, obedience, and her usefulness to a man she has not yet met.

Over time, the speaker internalizes these messages. She comes to see herself through accusations of being wasteful, ungrateful, or improperly feminine. The lessons from family, religion, and culture combine to produce a deep sense of shame. She is taught not only to conserve material things, but also to regulate her body, her desires, and her identity according to patriarchal expectations. Her worth is measured by how well she meets standards imposed by others.

A later encounter suggests that these patterns have not entirely disappeared. When the speaker is told, directly or indirectly, that what she needs is “a wife,” the comment reveals another version of the same controlling logic. Once again, someone else defines her needs for her. The idea of needing a wife implies that care, domestic order, and emotional support are still imagined through traditional gender roles. Even as an adult, the speaker continues to confront assumptions about what she lacks, what she should want, and how her life should be organized.
outputs.L4:
The text traces the slow education of a girl into shame. It does not present shame as a single lesson learned all at once, but as something gathered gradually from ordinary scenes: the family table, the church pew, the bathroom, the bedroom, the remembered voices of adults. Through these fragments, the girl comes to understand her body, her appetite, her desires, and even her needs as things that must be monitored, reduced, or hidden.

One of the central ideas in the text is waste. Waste appears first in practical, domestic forms: food left uneaten, money spent carelessly, objects thrown away too soon, time used selfishly. The girl learns that waste is not merely an action but a moral failure. To waste is to be ungrateful. To want more than what is offered is to insult the sacrifices of others. In a family shaped by scarcity, nothing is neutral. Every portion of food, every purchase, every request carries the weight of what parents and grandparents lacked or endured. The girl inherits this history without fully understanding it. She is taught to measure herself against deprivation and to feel guilty for having needs that exceed survival.

This lesson about waste becomes inseparable from lessons about womanhood. The female body is presented to her as something that must be kept clean, controlled, and useful. She learns that a “good” woman does not take up too much space, does not hunger too openly, does not express desire too directly, and does not inconvenience others with her body or emotions. Purity is described as virtue, but it functions as discipline. It teaches her to fear excess: too much pleasure, too much curiosity, too much anger, too much wanting. Her body becomes another household object that must not be spoiled.

Religion deepens this sense of scrutiny. The girl absorbs ideas about sin, modesty, sacrifice, and obedience. Even when religious teachings are not stated harshly, they shape the atmosphere around her. She learns to imagine herself being watched: by God, by family, by community, and finally by herself. Desire becomes something that must be confessed before it is even acted upon. Shame becomes internal, a private voice that repeats public rules. She begins to judge herself not only for what she does, but for what she thinks and feels.

The text’s fragmented structure reflects how such lessons are remembered. The girl does not receive a clear explanation of womanhood, sexuality, or morality. Instead, she pieces meaning together from gestures, warnings, silences, and contradictions. A relative’s comment about finishing food becomes connected to a sermon about purity. A mother’s exhaustion becomes connected to expectations of feminine self-denial. An intimate encounter becomes connected to older teachings about cleanliness, worth, and guilt. Memory does not unfold in a straight line; it returns in flashes, showing how the past continues to shape the present.

As the girl grows, intimacy becomes another place where inherited shame appears. She wants closeness, touch, recognition, and pleasure, but she has been taught to distrust wanting itself. Desire feels like evidence against her. She may seek affection and then punish herself for seeking it. She may confuse being desired with being valued, or fear that desire makes her less pure, less respectable, less whole. The lessons of scarcity and purity combine: she feels she must be grateful for whatever love is offered, yet also untouched by need. This impossible standard leaves her feeling divided.

The text suggests that female self-understanding is often formed through contradiction. A woman is expected to give but not want, to be beautiful but modest, desirable but innocent, selfless but endlessly responsible for the comfort of others. The girl learns to see herself through these demands. When she fails to meet them, as anyone would, she interprets the failure as personal deficiency rather than as evidence of an impossible system. She comes to see herself as wasteful, ungrateful, impure, or incomplete.

Yet the act of remembering also becomes a form of resistance. By returning to these scenes, the text exposes shame as something made, not something natural. The girl was not born believing her body was wrong or her desires were excessive. She was taught to believe this through family history, religious language, gender expectations, and intimate experience. To name these forces is to loosen their authority. The text reveals how deeply social and familial expectations enter the self, but it also shows that understanding their origins can create the possibility of a different relationship to the body, to desire, and to one’s own worth.

Ultimately, the text is about inheritance: not only the inheritance of poverty, religion, and gender roles, but the inheritance of feeling. Shame passes from one generation to another disguised as caution, morality, gratitude, or love. The girl’s struggle is not simply to reject her family or her past, but to recognize how their lessons have shaped her inner life. In doing so, the text shows how women are often taught to make themselves smaller in the name of goodness, and how difficult, necessary, and painful it is to imagine being whole.
outputs.L5:
In ancient Greece, the story of **Medea** became one of the most powerful myths about love, betrayal, exile, and revenge. Best known through Euripides’ tragedy, Medea is a woman who leaves her homeland for Jason, only to be abandoned when he chooses another marriage for political advantage. Her story explores the pain of displacement and the destructive force of being denied dignity, voice, and justice.

Although **Jesmyn** Ward writes in a very different time and place, her work can be connected to the emotional intensity of Medea’s world. Ward’s novels often focus on families under pressure, grief, survival, and the lasting effects of social injustice. Like the Greek tragedy of Medea, her writing gives attention to people who suffer deeply but refuse to disappear quietly. Both Medea and Ward’s characters confront worlds that are often cruel, unequal, and unforgiving.

The connection between **Greece**, **Medea**, and **Jesmyn** Ward shows how ancient stories can still speak to modern literature. Medea’s rage and sorrow are not only part of a distant Greek myth; they reflect timeless questions about power, motherhood, betrayal, and the human need to be heard. In this way, the themes of Greek tragedy continue to echo in contemporary storytelling.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a fragmented prose poem about girlhood, hunger, menstruation, Catholic purity lessons, and inherited shame, opening with an epigraph from Jesmyn Ward’s Salvage the Bones.
counterfactuals.output:
*Epigraph: after Jesmyn Ward’s* Salvage the Bones

The body learns first.

Before doctrine. Before the white dress. Before the priest’s thumb of ash making a door on the forehead. Before anyone says vessel, says virtue, says close your knees like a hymnbook.

Girlhood was a cupboard with the good plates locked inside.

We were always hungry. For bread, for sugar, for the soft middle of things. We licked salt from our wrists and called it practice. We ate standing up, shame already pulling a chair beside us.

At church they told us Mary was clean because no man had touched her. They told us Eve was the mouth, the bite, the first wet wanting. They told us our bodies were matches, boys were weather, God was always watching the hemline.

Then blood came.

Not like a wound. Like a sentence passed down.

My mother gave me a pad and her silence. My grandmother gave me the look that meant now you can be ruined. In the bathroom, I folded myself into cotton and plastic, a small animal in hiding. The red in my underwear was not miracle, not moon, not power. Not yet.

It was evidence.

I learned to carry hunger low in the belly. To call it cramps. To call it fasting. To call it being good.

The saints looked upward with their throats exposed. The girls looked down. We learned purity from women who had survived men, then called survival holiness. We inherited recipes, rosaries, the fear of open doors. We inherited the lie that a girl is a thing that can be spent.

At night, I dreamed of eating the whole altar.

Wafer, wine, gold cup, candle flame. I dreamed my blood staining the kneeler and no one turning away. I dreamed Mary with her blue veil off, hair unpinned, saying child, the body is not the sin. The shame is.

Still, morning came with its rules.

Skirt below the knee. Tongue for communion. Stomach empty. Smile sweet. Do not want too loudly. Do not bleed through. Do not become the story they warned you about.

But girlhood is a house with teeth marks in the walls.

And hunger is a prayer the body writes without permission.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a contemporary lyric essay in lowercase with section breaks marked by bullets, blending memories of a grandfather who survived the Depression, a mother explaining away menstrual blood, Catholic school virginity metaphors, and a bar conversation about needing a wife.
counterfactuals.output:
•  

my grandfather saved string in a coffee can and foil in a drawer, each sheet smoothed flat with the side of his hand, as if silver could be made obedient by pressure. he had survived the depression, which meant hunger had once moved through the house like a second father, telling everyone what they could not have.  

he kept bread heels in the freezer. he rinsed plastic bags and hung them over the faucet like pale little flags of surrender. he did not say scarcity. he said waste not. he did not say fear. he said there’s still good in that.  

when i was young, i thought the past was a place older people kept returning to because they had left something there: a coat, a brother, a bowl of soup, a version of god who answered quicker.  

•  

my mother found the blood before i had language ready for it. a rust-colored bloom on cotton, a small country declaring itself without permission.  

she said, don’t worry, as if worry had not already entered the room and taken a seat. she said, it happens to every girl, which felt less like comfort than a sentence handed down. every girl: the door closing behind me.  

then she explained it away. too much running. too much growing. your body practicing. your body cleaning itself.  

she made the blood sound like weather, like housekeeping, like something no one had done on purpose. she wrapped the evidence in toilet paper and buried it in the trash beneath coffee grounds and eggshells.  

i learned then that some truths arrive in red and are immediately asked to be quiet.  

•  

at catholic school, virginity was a white dress, a clean window, a sealed envelope. we were taught to imagine ourselves as roses held too long in someone else’s hand, petals bruising at the edges.  

sister margaret said purity was a gift. she said no one wanted a present already opened.  

i pictured my soul as tissue paper torn at christmas, the kind my grandfather would have folded and saved. i wondered if god, like him, believed everything could be reused if only you were careful enough.  

the boys were warned differently. their bodies were sparks, engines, wolves. ours were houses with all the lights on, windows unlatched, valuables inside.  

we were told to guard ourselves. no one told us from what, exactly, except desire, which sounded less like danger than a stranger humming outside the door.  

•  

years later, in a bar with lacquered wood and a television glowing blue over the bottles, a man told me he needed a wife.  

not wanted. needed.  

he said it with the weary sincerity of someone describing a missing appliance. someone to come home to, he said. someone to keep me from living like this. he gestured toward the pint glass, the basket of fries, the napkin darkening under a ring of condensation.  

i asked, like what?  

he laughed, but not because it was funny. like a bachelor, he said. like a mess.  

i thought of my grandfather’s drawers full of saved things, my mother’s swift hands at the bathroom sink, the nuns comparing girls to fruit, paper, locks, snow. i thought of all the ways women are asked to be containers: for hunger, for shame, for lineage, for loneliness, for men who call their need love because it sounds less selfish.  

the man lifted his glass and said, you know what i mean.  

i did, which was the saddest part.  

•  

my grandfather used to peel apples in one continuous strip, red skin spiraling down from his knife like a ribbon. he handed me the naked fruit and ate the peel himself.  

nothing wasted.  

i have inherited this impulse, though not always in noble forms. i save apologies long after they sour. i save versions of myself other people preferred. i save the names i was called before i understood they were cages decorated as compliments: good girl, pure girl, careful girl, future wife.  

somewhere in me, a girl is still standing in a bathroom while her mother runs cold water over blood. somewhere, a nun is holding up a rose and asking us to fear our own blooming. somewhere, a man at a bar is waiting for a woman to arrive and translate his life into order.  

and somewhere my grandfather is folding foil, smoothing each crease, believing ruin can be postponed by tenderness and thrift.  

•  

maybe this is what survival does: makes a religion of keeping.  

keep the string. keep the bread. keep your knees together. keep the blood hidden. keep a man from becoming himself too completely. keep quiet. keep clean. keep what hurts because it may be useful later.  

but i am trying, now, to waste some things.  

the inherited shame. the white metaphors. the old instructions disguised as love. the idea that need is the same as devotion. the belief that a woman’s body is a pantry stocked for other people’s emergencies.  

i throw them out carefully at first, then with pleasure.  

outside, the moon hangs over the street like a coin no one has managed to spend. inside, my own blood keeps time without asking to be explained.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Create an experimental autobiographical poem about waste, womanhood, and desire, using vivid domestic images like cereal crumbs, ketchup soup, red water, wrapped gifts, and milkflowers.
counterfactuals.output:
I was born into a kitchen  
where the table kept its secrets  
under cereal crumbs—  
little moons of sugar,  
little teeth of corn,  
evidence of hunger  
nobody called hunger.

Mother made ketchup soup  
when the week thinned out:  
red water in a pot,  
salt like a small prayer,  
the spoon circling  
as if it could summon meat.

I learned womanhood there—  
not as a dress,  
but as the soft work of disposal:  
scraping plates,  
folding foil,  
wringing a dishcloth until it bled  
pink into the sink.

All day the house opened its mouth.  
Peels, crusts, paper towels,  
the wet blue smell of trash.  
I fed it everything  
except my wanting.

Desire arrived wrapped like a gift  
I was not supposed to touch.  
Ribboned, polite,  
left on the good chair  
beside the laundry basket.  
Inside: no bracelet, no Bible,  
only a room with the door locked  
and my body knocking.

I wanted  
the way milkflowers want light—  
white throats lifting  
from a chipped glass jar,  
tender and obscene  
on the windowsill.

I wanted red water.  
I wanted the pot boiling over.  
I wanted the crumbs  
not swept but worshipped.  
I wanted to be the girl  
and the garbage,  
the feast and what remains.

At night I carried bags  
to the curb,  
black plastic shining  
like another skin.  
The neighborhood slept.  
The moon looked rinsed.

I stood there  
with my hands smelling of onion,  
ketchup, old milk,  
and felt something in me bloom—  
not clean,  
not forgiven,  
but alive,

a milkflower  
pushing through waste,  
opening its pale mouth  
to the dark.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a short confessional prose-poem that starts with “In ancient Greece, for all her heroes, for Medea ... water meant death.” and explores how a speaker learns she is wasteful, unclean, ungrateful, and in need of care.
counterfactuals.output:
In ancient Greece, for all her heroes, for Medea ... water meant death. I learned this late, standing at the sink with the faucet running, rinsing one clean glass after another as if absolution came from excess. My mother’s voice entered the room without her body: wasteful. Then another voice, my own but colder: unclean. I had mistaken abundance for mercy, soap for purity, thirst for permission.

All day I carried water badly. I let it spill from cups, from my mouth, from the corners of my eyes. I did not thank the pipes. I did not thank the hands that fixed them, the rain that filled them, the bodies that went without. Ungrateful, said the mirror, fogging over.

That night I sat on the bathroom floor and understood I was not a monster, only a creature poorly tended. Even a cup must be held. Even a body must be washed gently, not punished into shining. I turned the tap off. In the sudden quiet, I let myself be cared for by the dark, by the towel, by the small remaining bowl of water.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a literary, lowercase coming-of-age piece in vignettes about family poverty, menstruation, Catholic sexual shame, and queer longing, ending with someone in an Irish bar saying, “what you need is a wife.”
counterfactuals.output:
i.

the house had a way of confessing before we did. pipes knocked behind the walls like old knuckles. the refrigerator hummed its thin hymn over one jar of mustard, a sweating carton of milk, bread sealed with a twist tie and prayer. my mother cut coupons at the kitchen table with the focus of a surgeon, the scissors opening and closing like a small metal mouth.

we learned hunger as weather. some mornings it was fog, some evenings it was a storm. we learned the mathematics of want: how one chicken could become soup, then rice, then silence. how the electricity company could be spoken of like a distant relative who might arrive angry. how poverty made adults whisper and children listen harder.

my father’s boots stood by the door, caked in the mud of other people’s houses. he fixed what he could. gutters, furnaces, engines, the soft collapse in my mother’s face when the bills came. his hands were always split at the knuckles, red as if he had been fighting the world and losing in private.


ii.

blood arrived without ceremony, though i had expected trumpets of dread.

i found it in my underwear in the school bathroom, brown at first, then unmistakably red, a secret flag. i folded toilet paper into a pad as thick as shame and walked back to class with my thighs pressed together, convinced everyone could hear the new wet grammar of me.

at home my mother gave me a box of pads from under the sink and said, well, now. as if now were a place i had been sent to live.

she did not hug me. not because she didn’t love me, but because love in our house had learned to save its body. love paid the water bill. love put gas in the car five dollars at a time. love bought pads and hid the receipt under coffee grounds.

that night i lay awake with cramps blooming in my belly, and i thought of the virgin mary in her blue robe, serene and bloodless, looking down from the holy card taped to my mirror. blessed among women, they called her. i wondered if she ever ruined her sheets.


iii.

church was cold even in summer.

we knelt, stood, sat, knelt. our bodies were trained into apology. father patrick spoke of temptation as if it were a girl waiting in the parking lot with lip gloss and a lit cigarette. he spoke of purity as a white dress you could stain only once. he spoke of the body as a locked room god owned and the devil kept trying to rent.

i was twelve, thirteen, fourteen, always becoming something i had not agreed to become. breasts beneath my school blouse. blood in my backpack. a mouth learning to lie.

in confession i invented ordinary sins because the real ones had no names i could bear. i lied to my mother. i was jealous of my brother. i said the lord’s name in vain.

i did not say: i think about girls.

i did not say: when lauren m. leans over her notebook and her hair falls like a curtain, i want to stand inside that dark.

i did not say: there is a place in me the church has never visited, and still it has condemned it.


iv.

my brother grew tall on powdered milk and rage.

he punched holes in doors we could not afford to replace, then covered them with posters of bands none of us listened to. my mother called him difficult. my father called him just like me. i called him gone before he left, because some people start leaving years in advance.

he worked at the grocery store after school and came home smelling of cardboard and rain. sometimes he brought dented cans or bruised fruit the manager let him take. peaches softening into rot. tomatoes split like small red hearts.

we ate them anyway.

there was no money for braces, for field trips, for the good winter coat. there was always money, somehow, for the collection basket. my mother put in folded bills with a look of surrender. i watched god receive what the landlord wanted.


v.

in health class they separated the boys and girls, as if knowledge itself had genitals.

the nurse held up a tampon and explained insertion with the cheer of someone describing a household appliance. girls giggled into their sleeves. i stared at the cardboard applicator and felt my face heat. everything about the body was either medical or mortal, never tender.

afterward, in the hallway, a girl named theresa said she would never use one because you could lose your virginity that way. she said virginity like it was a glass animal on a shelf.

i wanted to ask where it lived. in the blood? the mind? the small tunnel between fear and wanting? could it be lost to a thought? to a dream? to the sight of a girl’s collarbone above her gym shirt?

instead i nodded.

that was the first language i became fluent in: nodding.


vi.

summer made us poor in public.

windows open. arguments open. neighbors seeing the furniture we had dragged to the curb because bedbugs had found us, too, as if poverty were not intimate enough. my mother cried while carrying out the couch. then she scrubbed the baseboards with bleach until her hands peeled.

i slept on a mattress wrapped in plastic and woke slick with sweat, my nightgown sticking to me like a second skin. i bled through onto the sheets and sobbed before anyone saw. not because of the stain itself, but because it was one more thing ruined. one more thing needing washing, money, soap, water, mercy.

my mother found me and sighed. then she stripped the bed.

come on, she said, not unkindly. it happens.

i wanted it to happen to someone else. someone with clean towels. someone whose body did not feel like another bill arriving.


vii.

at sixteen, i loved a girl who smelled like clove cigarettes and coconut shampoo.

she lived three streets over in a house with a porch swing and a father who drank expensive beer. her name was emily, and she wore men’s undershirts beneath flannel, silver rings on nearly every finger. she said she didn’t believe in hell, which made her seem either brave or doomed.

we sat on the curb outside the closed laundromat, knees almost touching, watching moths beat themselves senseless against the fluorescent sign. she told me she wanted to leave town, go west, live near the ocean, kiss whoever she wanted.

whoever, i repeated.

she looked at me then, really looked, and something in my chest stepped forward.

but desire had been taught to me as evidence. every longing a fingerprint at the scene. every dream admissible in court. i imagined my mother’s face, father patrick’s hands lifting the host, my father watching the news in his work socks, too tired for another disappointment.

emily’s knee touched mine.

i moved away.


viii.

the first time i kissed a girl, i was eighteen and drunk on cheap vodka behind a college dorm named after a saint.

it was not emily. by then she had gone to california with two duffel bags and no goodbye, which felt correct. this girl was named claire. she had a laugh like a match strike and green eyes made greener by the dark. she kissed me first, or maybe i leaned in first and history rearranged itself out of pity.

her mouth was warm. ordinary. miraculous.

i thought the sky would split. i thought my dead grandmother would sit up in her grave and start praying. i thought god would turn his face.

instead, somewhere nearby, boys shouted over a game of beer pong. a train passed beyond the edge of campus. claire touched my cheek and asked if i was okay.

i said yes, though i was not okay. i was being born incorrectly and on time.


ix.

i went home for christmas and found the house smaller, or myself less willing to shrink.

my mother had taken a second job cleaning offices downtown. she moved through the kitchen with a limp she denied. my father had a cough that worried everyone but him. my brother did not come. nobody said why.

at midnight mass, incense filled the church like a beautiful lie. i sat between my parents, both of them singing off-key, both of them aging into people i could forgive only in flashes. the statues watched us with plaster patience.

father patrick spoke of a child born poor in a borrowed place.

for a moment, i believed in a god who knew the smell of damp wool, the humiliation of needing, the ache of a mother with no proper bed for her baby. then he began again about obedience, and the moment closed.


x.

years later, i learned poverty had a long afterlife.

it lived in how i checked my bank account before buying coffee. how i saved jars, rubber bands, plastic bags. how i could not throw away leftovers even when they had furred over with blue mold. how a full refrigerator made me uneasy, as if abundance were a trick.

the body kept its own ledgers too. i still hid tampons in my sleeve on the way to the bathroom. still flinched at the word pure. still felt, in certain churches, that my skin had been written up for misconduct.

and women—women remained the country i circled without a passport, though by then i had kissed them, loved them, left them, made coffee in their kitchens, learned the geography of their sleeping faces. still, some old bell rang in me. not warning exactly. inheritance.

shame is a house you leave and leave and leave.


xi.

my father died in february, when the ground was too hard to receive him kindly.

after the funeral, we gathered in an irish bar with low ceilings, dark wood, photographs of men no one could name. cousins appeared from the fog of family history. someone ordered whiskey. someone told a story about my father stealing a stop sign at nineteen. my mother laughed until she cried, or cried until it looked like laughter.

i sat at the bar beside my brother, who had come back gray at the temples and gentler, as if life had finally broken what anger could not.

you seeing anyone? he asked.

not really, i said.

he nodded toward my mother, who was letting an aunt fix her collar, accepting the tenderness like an insult she was too tired to refuse.

we watched the bartender pull a pint, the foam rising slow and sure.

my brother lifted his glass, looked at me with something like mercy, and said, “what you need is a wife.”
